dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — Benji is five days old, and it's a cold, damp Friday to stay in with him. Overnight, Iran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar tied to seven demands, while tankers keep getting hit in the Strait of Hormuz, and chip stocks are bouncing this morning after Thursday's 5.52% Nasdaq drop into correction. Solon tops out near 49° with temperatures falling through the day and showers likely by evening, so any errands are better done early. Tonight is a sports doubleheader from the couch: Ohio State hoops opens at home against Youngstown State at 6:30 PM, and the Cavs host the 8-1 76ers at 7:30 PM in an NBA Cup game, with Jarrett Allen questionable. Locally, the Ohio Hazmat Teams Conference runs today and tomorrow at the Solon Community Center.

weekBrief.text: Benji's first week wraps up as a quiet, stay-home stretch — born Sunday, home Tuesday, pediatrician Wednesday, and now five days old with the house settling into a rhythm around him. Solon's weather turns cold and damp for the weekend — 49° with evening showers Friday and 46° Saturday — then breaks sunny and warmer Sunday at 57°, peaking near 61° Tuesday before cooling again. The sports weekend is stacked: the Cavs host Philadelphia tonight and the Knicks Saturday, Ohio State football hosts Oregon Saturday afternoon, and the Browns visit the Saints Sunday with Shedeur Sanders in line for his first start of the season. The week's standout grocery move stays the Thanksgiving stock-up — Meijer brand frozen turkeys at 79¢/lb or less through November 26 beat Giant Eagle's 95¢/lb — and if energy allows, Hadestown continues at Playhouse Square this weekend.

Trump calls Qatar's emir as diplomacy races to head off new Iran strikes
items.summary:
President Trump spoke by phone on Friday with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani about efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war, according to Qatar's Amiri Diwan. The call came a day after Trump told reporters he would soon decide whether to resume major military operations.

Qatar has been the main go-between in the conflict, and it was through Doha that Iran passed its nuclear proposal to Washington this week. The emir stressed keeping dialogue open, avoiding further escalation, and protecting shipping and energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.

The timing is the story: both tracks are live at once. Mediators are pushing an interim arrangement that would reopen shipping in exchange for easing the blockade and other restrictions, while U.S. forces continue preparing options if talks stall.

What to watch is whether the Qatar channel produces a written interim step in the next few days, or whether Washington signals that the military option is moving first.

items.title: Iran reportedly asks Russia for S-400 air defences in a letter to Putin
items.summary:
Iran has reportedly asked Russia for S-400 air-defence systems as it works to rebuild defences damaged in the war, according to reporting cited by Iran International from The Telegraph and a senior Iranian official. The request was said to be in a personal message from Mojtaba Khamenei to President Vladimir Putin.

The message was reportedly delivered during a Moscow visit this week by senior security official Mohsen Rezaei. Public accounts of that visit focused on regional security talks, and neither a completed sale nor a delivery timetable has been confirmed.

Even a request matters. Air defence has been one of Iran's clearest vulnerabilities, and stronger systems would change the calculation for any renewed U.S. or Israeli strikes.

Watch for any Russian confirmation. A reported ask is not a shipment, and Moscow has not said it will supply the systems or intervene directly.

items.title: Zelenskiy warns Russia is planning new strikes on energy, bridges and civilian sites
items.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Friday that intelligence points to new Russian strikes on energy targets, bridges across the Dnipro River, and civilian infrastructure. He said Ukraine's air force and armed forces are preparing to defend against them.

Kyiv and other cities have faced near-constant attacks for weeks, and two major bridges in the capital were hit late last month. Zelenskiy repeated his call for allies to move faster on missiles for the U.S.-made Patriot system.

That supply problem remains stark: Washington recently approved a sale of 500 Patriot missiles valued at about $2.1 billion, but deliveries are not expected until the early 2030s, well after the current phase of the war.

Talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States are due to resume next week, so the next strikes — and the air-defence response — will land in the middle of diplomacy.

items.title: Ukraine says it will keep hitting Russia's oil refining sector
items.summary:
Ukraine is continuing attacks on targets tied to Russia's oil refining industry, Zelenskiy said on Friday, describing them as a response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities. He made the comment after reviewing a report on Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets.

Russian officials have reported several strikes on oil industry sites in the past week, including in the Samara and Yaroslavl regions and around Ryazan, though Ukrainian officials have not claimed each one specifically. Ukrainian power plants, heating and water systems remain under repeated attack at the same time.

President Trump has asked Ukraine several times to halt the refinery attacks, saying they push diesel prices higher. Zelenskiy has said Kyiv is ready to stop if Russia stops hitting energy targets.

The exchange sets up a clear test for next week's talks: a mutual pause on energy strikes is one of the few concrete de-escalation steps either side has actually named.

items.title: Zelenskiy says Ukraine must adapt to Washington's new politics — and solve its Patriot shortage
items.summary:
Zelenskiy says Ukraine has to adjust to the changed political landscape in the United States after the midterms and build a working dialogue to keep aid and air defences flowing. He made the comments in an interview broadcast Thursday while attending a summit in Spain.

His most urgent problem, he said, is Patriot air-defence missiles, calling it the number one priority and warning that things get very tough without a solution. He also says Ukraine is still owed about $16 billion in assistance that Washington promised but did not deliver, and is working to keep enough F-16s flying over the next several months.

The backdrop is awkward: the State Department recently approved a sale of 500 Patriot missiles worth about $2.1 billion, but deliveries are not expected until the early 2030s — far too late for the current war. U.S.-led talks involving Ukraine and Russia are scheduled to resume next week in Abu Dhabi.

What to watch is whether the new Congress moves any faster on Ukraine aid than the outgoing one, and whether the Abu Dhabi round produces anything concrete.

items.title: Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles, after the midterm rout
items.summary:
President Trump announced on Friday that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff starting Monday, November 9. Wiles, the first woman to hold the job, will move to Trump's political operation.

The move is the first major personnel shake-up since Republicans lost both chambers of Congress on Tuesday. Reporting on Friday described Trump growing angrier as coverage of the losses sank in, and Wiles was said to have submitted her resignation on Thursday evening.

Miller, currently a deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, has been the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration agenda and has steadily widened his role across domestic policy. His promotion signals continuity on policy, not a pivot, even as the staff leadership changes.

Watch how the new Democratic Congress responds. A Miller-led White House and a Democratic House and Senate point to a confrontational two years, starting with oversight and war-powers fights.

items.title: Races still uncalled on Friday — Alaska and Mississippi will set the size of the Democratic majorities
items.summary:
Three days after Election Day, votes are still being counted in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races and in dozens of House contests, and officials warn final counts could take days or weeks. Democrats have already won control of both the House and the Senate.

In North Carolina, Democrats have flipped the state's House delegation, going from holding four of 14 seats to at least nine, with two races still extremely close — one Republican leading by 233 votes and another trailing by 99 votes. Provisional, corrected mail and military ballots are still being reviewed.

Across the country, Democrats also flipped five governor's offices — Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada and Texas — with a sixth possible in Alaska. Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms announced a transition team on Friday that includes filmmaker Tyler Perry.

The remaining calls will decide how much room Democratic leaders actually have. A seat or two in the Senate, in particular, changes what can pass and what can be blocked.

items.title: The new Democratic Congress is preparing investigations — and companies are lawyering up
items.summary:
With Democrats set to hold at least 250 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats in January, incoming committee leaders are preparing to use subpoena power to investigate the administration, the president's family and their business ventures, according to a detailed legal analysis published Friday.

That is a sharp reversal from the last two years, when Republican majorities aimed much of their oversight at private companies and institutions they associated with the political left. The new majority is expected to target the executive branch directly, while also pulling in companies as witnesses and sources.

House Democrats have scheduled leadership elections for November 18 and 19, with Hakeem Jeffries the presumptive Speaker and Chuck Schumer the presumptive Senate Majority Leader. Both have framed their first priorities around affordability and accountability.

Lawyers are advising companies to prepare during the lame-duck session, before the first letters arrive in January — a sign the oversight wave is being treated as certain, not hypothetical.

items.title: Iowa's newest congresswoman-elect heads to Washington focused on costs and health care
items.summary:
Democratic Rep.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott, who unseated two-term Republican Rep. Zach Nunn in Iowa, told reporters on Friday she is ready to get to work in a House majority of at least 256 and a Senate majority of 54. She travels to Washington on November 8 for orientation.

Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister, campaigned on ending sweeping tariffs and the Iran war, improving health care and tackling corruption. She says she wants to reverse Medicaid cuts, restore enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and support a public health care option, and hopes for an agriculture or health care committee seat.

She is part of a notable wave: several newly elected members are clergy, including Iowa's Lindsay James and Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. She also pledged regular open town halls in every county in her district.

Her test starts January 3, when she is sworn in. Democrats will still need a Republican president's signature to turn most promises into law, which makes early bipartisan deals the thing to watch.

items.title: What Amy Acton's win means for Ohio schools and the EdChoice voucher fight
items.summary:
Governor-elect Amy Acton's victory is about to collide with education policy in Columbus. Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected Ohio governor and the first Democrat to win the office in 20 years, and schools were a central part of the campaign debate.

The legislature she will face is still Republican, but not as dominant as before. Republicans entered the election with a 65-34 Ohio House majority that allowed veto overrides; Democratic gains on Tuesday will drop them below the 60-seat supermajority they have held since 2013.

That shift matters most on contested programs like EdChoice school vouchers and school funding, where a governor's veto could now actually stick. It sets up divided government in Ohio for the first time in years, with education as an early battleground.

Watch Acton's first budget proposal. That document, more than campaign speeches, will show how much of her education agenda she thinks she can get through a Republican legislature.

items.title: How a blue tsunami happened — and why Republicans say they could not blame fraud
items.summary:
Journalism looking back at election week describes a result that went well beyond a normal midterm correction: Democrats flipped previously red strongholds including South Carolina, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, and built their largest House position in a generation.

Reporting based on more than 70 interviews inside both campaigns concluded that Republicans could not overcome a president who had lost public trust on the economy and other issues. Exit polling cited this week put Trump's approval at 38 percent, with most voters saying tariffs hurt the economy and 63 percent calling the Iran war the wrong decision.

Texas became the emblem race, electing a Democratic governor for the first time since the 1990s and sending Democrat James Talarico to the Senate over Ken Paxton. At the same time, analysts caution that the Democratic advantage on the economy was relatively slim and many of its voters still view the party unfavorably.

That tension is the story of the next two years: a sweeping win built more on rejection of the president than enthusiasm for the winners, which leaves the new majority with something to prove quickly.

items.title: Markets close mixed Friday: Nasdaq up 1.09% as chips bounce, Dow down 0.46%
items.summary:
Wall Street closed mixed on Friday after Thursday's historic selloff. The Nasdaq Composite finished up 1.09% at 24,579.43, the S&P 500 rose 0.31% to 7,376.86, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46% to 51,285.73.

Semiconductors led the recovery. Micron rose about 5% after plunging 17% the day before, and Nvidia climbed about 2% after Thursday's 9% drop, turning its year-to-date return positive again. Bargain hunting in AI names drove most of the rebound.

Even with Friday's gain, the Nasdaq remains more than 10% below its recent high, in correction territory. The week's losses were triggered by fears that Democratic control of Congress could bring tighter rules on AI data-center construction.

Traders expect volatility to continue. The next tests are whether chip stocks can hold their gains on Monday and how the Federal Reserve talks about rates after the strong jobs report.

items.title: Chip stocks pare their losses — but the jobs report revives rate-hike fears
items.summary:
Chip stocks came into Friday trying to recover from the Nasdaq's steepest one-day decline in 19 months, a selloff sparked by fears that a Democratic-led Congress could mean tougher AI regulation and slower data-center buildout. The index was also headed for a fourth straight weekly fall.

Premarket and early trading showed broad relief in semiconductors, with Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Broadcom and Micron all up between roughly 5% and 9% at points, and Tesla and SpaceX also rebounding after two rough sessions. Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX, eased slightly to around 26.7 after its biggest one-day jump in about 19 months.

The complication was the jobs report. Stronger-than-expected hiring pushed traders to raise the odds of a December Fed rate hike to about 78%, from around 70% earlier — the opposite of the relief a beaten-down tech sector wanted.

So Friday was two stories at once: a genuine bounce in the stocks that were hit hardest, and a macro backdrop that got less friendly while it happened.

items.title: October hiring crushes expectations: 165,000 jobs added, unemployment down to 4.1%
items.summary:
Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, nearly three times the 59,000 economists expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1% from 4.2%.

Professional and business services led with 70,000 new jobs, well above its recent average, while health care added 42,000 and transportation and warehousing added 25,000, including strong gains for couriers and messengers. August and September were also revised higher, to 186,000 and 60,000.

Wages rose 0.4% for the month and 3.1% over the year. Participation held roughly steady at 61.9%, and long-term unemployment was little changed at about 2.0 million people.

The strength cuts both ways: it undercuts talk of a weakening economy, but it also strengthens the case for the Fed to raise rates in December. October inflation data, due Tuesday, is the next big input.

items.title: Investors balk at a $1.5 trillion price tag for Anthropic's IPO
items.summary:
Anthropic's planned stock market debut is facing pushback before the roadshow has even begun. Prospective investors are questioning a valuation discussed around $1.5 trillion and asking for a lower price before they commit, according to Reuters reporting citing people familiar with the talks.

Some investors involved in the discussions think the value is closer to $1 trillion, and one expects the offering could raise about $80 billion instead of the anticipated $100 billion. The roadshow was expected to start the week of November 9, with pricing the following week.

The timing could hardly be worse for a giant AI listing: this week's selloff hit AI valuations across the board, and investors are also waiting on Anthropic's October revenue figure, which was left blank in its updated filing. The company's revenue run rate reportedly topped $80 billion at the end of October.

Anthropic declined to comment. Watch for an amended filing with a price range — that document will show whether the company concedes on price or risks delaying the deal.

items.title: Cloudflare jumps nearly 10% after revenue surges 39% on AI network demand
items.summary:
Cloudflare shares opened about 17% higher on Friday and closed up 9.91% at $268.75, a sharp reversal from Thursday's 8% slide in the tech selloff. The trigger was a third-quarter report that beat expectations on both the top and bottom lines.

Revenue rose 39% year over year to about $783 million, ahead of the roughly $737 million analysts expected, and adjusted earnings came in at $0.38 a share versus $0.34 expected. The company also guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $845 million to $846 million.

Management tied the growth to surging demand for AI-related network infrastructure and a developer base that has doubled to about 10 million. The caution in the numbers is margin: gross margin slipped as Cloudflare spends ahead of the traffic it expects to carry.

For a market punishing AI spending without proof, Cloudflare offered the proof — actual accelerating revenue. Whether margins stabilize at the new guide is the question analysts flagged next.

items.title: Oil is set for its steepest weekly fall since 2020 — Brent down about 16%
items.summary:
Oil prices steadied on Friday but remained on track for a brutal week. Brent crude was set for a decline of about 16% for the week, its steepest percentage fall since the start of the COVID pandemic and its largest dollar drop in records going back to 1988, with U.S. crude down more than 13%.

The selloff followed the midterm results: Democratic control of Congress raised hopes of de-escalation in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which would mean more crude exports from the region. Prices fell about 8% on Wednesday alone, settling at two-month lows, and analysts pointed to a growing supply surplus building in September and October.

What kept prices from falling further was shipping. Attacks on vessels in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz are still running near record pace, and a seafarer was killed in a November 5 explosion aboard an oil-products tanker believed to have been hit by a missile.

Oil is now a direct bet on diplomacy: a credible interim deal keeps pressure on prices, while any return to strikes would likely snap them back above $100 quickly.

items.title: Most of Newsom's 548 death-row commutations still need California's Supreme Court
items.summary:
Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute all 548 California death sentences to life without parole hit its legal reality on Friday: he can act on his own for 166 people, but 382 cases first need a recommendation from the California Supreme Court.

Under the state constitution, clemency for someone with two or more felony convictions requires at least four of the court's seven justices to concur, and the court currently has a vacant seat. Newsom has asked the justices to act by the end of the year so he can finish before his term ends in January.

Newsom, who imposed an execution moratorium in 2019, argues the death penalty is unjust and error-prone. Law enforcement critics, including Riverside County's sheriff and district attorney, blasted the move and said victims' families and prosecutors were not consulted.

If the court signs off, it would be the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history. If it does not, the plan shrinks to the 166 cases the governor can do alone.

items.title: U.S. measles total tops 5,100 in the deadliest week of the year so far
items.summary:
Confirmed measles cases in the United States have reached 5,182, with 330 new infections reported this week, according to CDC figures summarized on Friday. It is the 13th straight week with a triple-digit national increase.

Only five states have reported no cases in 2026. Health departments in New York and Wisconsin reported measles-associated deaths this week — a child and an infant — making it the deadliest week for the disease this year.

Ohio is among the states reporting higher counts than federal tallies, at about 311 cases, concentrated in the northeast corner of the state in Geauga, Ashtabula and Wayne counties. Indiana also saw a sizable jump, while Kentucky added only a few cases.

Measles was once declared eliminated in the United States, and this year's total is the highest in decades. Health officials continue to point to vaccination coverage as the dividing line between contained clusters and statewide outbreaks.

items.title: A Lakewood, Colorado officer is killed and three are wounded in a bus shootout
items.summary:
A Lakewood police officer was killed and three other officers were wounded Thursday evening in a shootout involving a Regional Transportation District bus in the Denver suburb, authorities said Friday. A bystander was also injured, and the gunman was killed by police.

Officers responded around 6:30 p.m. to a call about a suspicious person trying to board a bus near Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard. Police say the man, who may have been involved in a hit-and-run earlier that day, opened fire when officers boarded, and officers fired back.

The three surviving officers were in stable condition at local hospitals on Thursday night. Names of the officer who died, the wounded and the gunman have not been released.

The Jefferson County Critical Incident Response Team is leading the investigation, with help from the Colorado Bureau of Investigation. Gov. Jared Polis ordered flags at half-staff for the fallen officer's memorial.

items.title: Behind the strong jobs number: part-time work for economic reasons jumps by 339,000
items.summary:
October's headline hiring beat came with a softer underside. The number of people working part time because they could not get full-time hours rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million, even as overall payrolls grew by 165,000.

A broader measure of joblessness that counts those workers and people who have stopped looking rose to 7.9%. The typical spell of unemployment has also lengthened, to about 11.9 weeks, suggesting people who lose work are taking longer to land again.

None of that erases the headline: unemployment fell to 4.1% and hiring was far stronger than forecast, with upward revisions to August and September. It does explain why a good report can still feel thin to households focused on hours and grocery prices.

October inflation data arrives Tuesday, November 10. Together, the two reports will shape whether the Fed sees an economy strong enough to justify another rate increase in December.

items.title: Airbnb jumps 12% and Moderna gains as earnings winners buck the week's rout
items.summary:
Friday's market had clear winners hiding inside a rough week. Airbnb shares jumped about 12% after the company beat expectations and raised guidance, and Moderna gained about 5% after a third-quarter result that handily beat forecasts.

Moderna reported about $200 million in profit on roughly $1.2 billion to $1.3 billion in revenue, against expectations for a large loss, helped by seasonal flu, COVID and RSV vaccine sales. It raised its full-year outlook to revenue growth of 15% to 25%. Airbnb posted earnings of $3.16 a share on $4.87 billion in revenue, both above consensus.

Not everything rose: DraftKings plunged about 21% on Friday, a reminder that investors are rewarding proven guidance and punishing misses hard in the current mood. Cloudflare, IonQ and Humana were also among the day's gainers.

The pattern matters for next week: after a valuation-driven selloff, actual results are deciding individual stocks again, one report at a time.

items.title: Browns name Shedeur Sanders the starter for Sunday at New Orleans
items.summary:
The Browns made it official on Friday: Shedeur Sanders will start at quarterback Sunday against the Saints, head coach Todd Monken announced. Deshaun Watson remains in concussion protocol and is listed as questionable.

Watson returned to practice Friday in a limited capacity after missing Wednesday and Thursday, but he has not cleared protocol, and Monken would not commit to him serving as the backup. Sanders took the first-team reps all week. In limited action this season he is 3-for-3 passing for 2 yards in two games, after starting seven games as a rookie last year.

Watson has led Cleveland to a 5-3 record, completing 65.5% of his passes for 1,806 yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions. Tight end Harold Fannin Jr., dealing with a groin issue, was cleared and is not on the final injury report.

Sunday is a genuine audition and a risk at once: a win keeps the surprising Browns in the AFC race, while the trade deadline arrives Tuesday with the quarterback picture still unsettled.

items.title: LeBron James plays in Cleveland tonight as a 76er for the first time — and Dean Wade expects a 'madhouse'
items.summary:
Rocket Arena hosts one of the season's strangest homecomings on Friday night: LeBron James playing in Cleveland as a member of the Philadelphia 76ers for the first time, in an Emirates NBA Cup game tipping at 7:30 p.m. on Prime Video.

Former Cav Dean Wade, now a Sixer himself, said he expects a madhouse, recalling that every James return in his seven years in Cleveland was crazy. Wade signed a four-year, $38 million deal with Philadelphia in June; James followed on July 24, choosing the Sixers over the Cavs and other suitors.

The basketball matters too. Philadelphia arrives 8-1 on a five-game winning streak, while Cleveland is 4-4 and 3-1 at home, still stinging from blowing a 29-point lead in a 114-106 opening-night loss in Philadelphia. Jarrett Allen, Tyrese Proctor and Peyton Watson were all listed as questionable for the Cavs.

Cleveland also made a roster move Friday, signing forward Norchad Omier to a two-way contract and waiving Riley Minix. After tonight, the Cavs host the Knicks on Saturday, so the weekend is a back-to-back test.

items.title: Ohio State hosts Oregon Saturday with a freshman at quarterback and playoff stakes on the line
items.summary:
No. 11 Ohio State (6-2) hosts No. 23 Oregon (5-3) at Ohio Stadium on Saturday at 3:30 p.m. on CBS, in a Big Ten game both teams need for their College Football Playoff hopes. Ohio State has designated it a 'Scarlet the Shoe' game.

The Buckeyes will again be without starting quarterback Julian Sayin, out with the elbow injury he suffered at Indiana, and running back Ja'Kobi Jackson. Freshman Luke Fahey makes his second straight start after completing 21 of 38 passes for 260 yards and a touchdown in the 30-18 loss at USC, feeding Jeremiah Smith for 10 catches and his Big Ten-record 40th career touchdown.

Oregon is in the same spot, starting Dylan Raiola with Dante Moore out with a concussion, and will miss leading rusher Jordon Davison. Ohio State is favored by about 7.5 points at home.

Ryan Day confirmed Fahey is the starter and said the locker room believes in him. With Sayin's return not expected soon, Saturday is less a spot start than the beginning of Ohio State's stretch run with a freshman.

items.title: Ohio measles cases are up nearly 600% this year, now in 25 counties
items.summary:
Ohio has reported 310 measles cases in 25 counties so far in 2026, according to the Ohio Department of Health dashboard updated November 5 — nearly six times the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. The state added 14 new cases in the past week.

Ashland County reported seven new cases, bringing its total to eight, and Mercer County joined the list with four cases. Earlier outbreaks this year hit Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February, and the current spread is the state's third outbreak of 2026.

Nationally, measles cases have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eliminated in the United States, with more than 5,000 cases reported this year. Northeast Ohio counties including Geauga, Ashtabula and Wayne have been among the state's heaviest-hit areas.

Health officials continue to urge vaccination checks, especially for families in affected counties. Symptoms can take up to three weeks to appear after exposure, so this month's exposures may not show in state counts until later in November.

items.title: Northeast Ohio voters backed the big Cuyahoga levies — and flipped a congressional seat
items.summary:
Cuyahoga County voters passed both major levies on Tuesday and approved three charter changes, according to unofficial results reviewed this week. Issue 10, the developmental disabilities levy, won with nearly 63%, and Issue 11, the health and human services levy, won with about 60%.

Together the levies add about $166.50 a year per $100,000 of property value. The charter issues — 12, 13 and 14 — limit some county executive powers, reshaping how the county government operates going forward.

In the region's biggest political upset, Democrat Brian Poindexter unseated Republican Rep. Max Miller in the 7th District with about 53% of the vote, part of a statewide night in which Amy Acton won the governor's office and Sherrod Brown won back a Senate seat.

Results remain unofficial until counties certify them; Cuyahoga County's certification is scheduled for November 24. Downtown, the foreclosure auction of the Huntington Building at 925 Euclid Ave. has also been pushed to November 10.

items.title: FBI announces arrest of a Brunswick man on federal child sexual abuse charges
items.summary:
The FBI's Cleveland division announced on Friday the federal arrest of Leonard Paul Funk Jr., 45, of Brunswick, Ohio, following an investigation led by the FBI Akron Resident Agency with Brunswick police, the Medina County Sheriff's Office, Tiffin police and Allegheny County police in Pennsylvania.

Authorities say the conduct described in the federal complaint spanned from the Toledo area to Pittsburgh. Funk is a registered Tier 1 sex offender with the Medina County Sheriff's Office.

He was located and arrested at his Brunswick home on Wednesday, November 4, and placed into federal custody without incident. He had his initial appearance in federal court in Ohio the same day, and the complaint has been unsealed.

The FBI notes that a complaint is an allegation and further details beyond the affidavit are not being released. Questions were directed to the FBI Cleveland public affairs office.

baby.tip: Day 5 tip — the paperwork one, while it's quiet: Benji needs to be added to the health plan, and newborn enrollment windows are usually short, so it's worth a call to the fund office to confirm the exact deadline and what they need (typically the birth certificate or hospital record). One short call now beats a scramble later — and ask his pediatrician's office what they need on file too.
baby.fact: At five days old, Benji already knows his favorite scent — newborns can recognize their mother's smell within days of birth and will turn toward it. His hearing is tuned the same way: the voices he's heard most, yours and Kelly's, are the ones that settle him fastest.
baby.fun: Name tidbit for Day 5: Benjamin means 'son of the right hand' in Hebrew — traditionally the favored spot. Tiny mission to match: one photo today of Benji in someone's right-arm cradle hold, Moose supervising from a polite distance.
